title: Who really knows?
hookLine: the Hymn of Creation ends: perhaps even the highest does not know
carry: it ends where it ends, on a question

cards: Where did everything come from? Children ask it at bedtime, and adults ask it at three in the morning. In the Rig Veda, a collection of hymns held sacred in Hindu tradition, a short hymn sets out to answer it too.

It's known as the Nasadiya hymn, the Hymn of Creation. It begins in the dark before anything, builds slowly toward the first stirring, and then, at the very end, does something surprising for a hymn. It asks.

teach.h: NEITHER WHAT IS NOR WHAT IS NOT.
teach.b: First, before the beginning. The hymn opens with a strange double negative: then there was neither what is nor what is not. No air, no sky beyond it.
It wonders what covered everything, and where, and whether there was deep water. Death wasn't there, and neither was deathlessness. No sign of night or day.
Darkness, it says, was hidden by darkness. Second, the stirring. Into that, something moves.

That One, the hymn says, breathed without breath, by its own nature. Desire arose in it, and desire was the first seed of mind. And sages, searching in their hearts, found the tie between what is and what is not.
Third, the doubt. Then the hymn turns and asks directly: who really knows? Who here can say where this creation came from?
The gods, it points out, came after the creation of the world. So who knows how it arose? Fourth, the ending.
The last verse names one possible witness: the one who watches over it from the highest heaven. Surely he knows.

teach.h: OR PERHAPS HE DOES NOT KNOW.
teach.b: And then the final words: or perhaps he does not know.
A sacred hymn about the beginning of everything, and its last move is to leave the question standing. Some readers hear humility there. Some hear the edge of what words can do.
The hymn itself doesn't say which. It ends where it ends, on a question.

how: The Nasadiya hymn (Rig Veda 10.129) is recited in Vedic chanting and studied in Hindu philosophy, where some readers take its closing doubt as a mark of humility before the question of origins.

games.q: you're the poet. you've sung the beginning of everything, from the dark to the first stirring. how do you end?
o: with the names of the gods who made it.
with: perhaps even the highest does not know.
games.why: the hymn ends with a question left open: the one in the highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps he does not know.

practice: Choose one question you can't settle, where all this came from, what happens after, why there's anything at all, and ask it once, slowly, inwardly.

When an answer starts to form, set it down, the way the hymn sets down its own, and keep the question open, like a door held for someone you can't see yet. If you pray, you can bring the question as it is.
